title: A stranger’s eyes
text: Dumas jumps forward to 1838 and hands the story to Franz, a young man who knows nothing of Dantès. We know far more than he does. We watched the treasure come out of the ground, and we heard the Englishman of the last chapter go by the name Sinbad, so the pleasure here is dramatic irony: we watch an outsider try to make sense of a man we already know.

title: A surname that should ring a bell
text: Franz’s travelling companion is the Viscount Albert de Morcerf. Caderousse has already told us who the Count de Morcerf is and whom he married. Dumas does not underline it. He trusts you to make the connection while Franz, who knows nothing of the old story, chats on.

title: The treasure cave becomes a palace
text: Sinbad, Aladdin, a mute servant, a hidden door: the whole evening is staged as a tale from the Arabian Nights. The bare grotto where Dantès dug for the chest has become a palace of brocade and marble. Notice that the wealth is not just spent but performed. Its job is to dazzle a visitor.

title: Why does he laugh?
text: Sinbad talks of vows still to be kept and of handing out his own secret justice. When Franz guesses at revenge, his host laughs it off. Is the laugh a denial, a mask, or a sign that the word is too small for what he means?

title: Dream and waking
text: Franz wakes on heather in a plain cave, and the hidden door cannot be found. Smoke marks show that others have searched before him. Dumas leaves it unclear how much of the night was real. Part of this man’s power is that nobody can check up on him.

title: On the side of hunted men
text: Instead of sailing for Malaga, Sinbad goes out of his way to land two Corsican bandits safely. Gaetano says he fears neither God nor devil and will always help a man on the run. Think of who he once was: a man the law locked up without a trial. Now his sympathy lies with the people the law is chasing.

title: What money cannot buy
text: Albert goes to bed sure that a full purse will find him a carriage in Carnival week. Pastrini says it cannot be done. In the same breath we learn that a very rich, foreign gentleman has taken the rest of the floor. Dumas has set out two kinds of wealth side by side: Albert’s, and something on a much grander scale.

title: A tale inside the tale
text: The novel stops for a whole chapter so that an innkeeper can tell a bandit romance. Dumas loves these nested stories. This one is not a detour. Like Dantès, Vampa is a gifted poor boy who teaches himself, steps outside the law and becomes a power in his own right, and the passing traveller called Sinbad ties his story to ours.

title: Gold in Teresa’s eyes
text: Teresa refuses Cucumetto’s gold, but her eyes light up at the sight of it. She longs to dance among the nobles. The night of the ball a fire breaks out, and next day Vampa gives her Carmela’s costume and jewels. Dumas never says outright how he came by them. Watch how desire for finery drives the people in this story.

title: Is there honor among bandits?
text: Carlini stabs the woman he loves rather than leave her to the band. Vampa kills his chief to save Teresa, then puts on the dead man’s clothes and takes his place. The bandits keep a strict code of their own. Is Vampa a hero, a monster, or something the ordinary words do not fit?

title: Behind the pillar
text: Franz hides in the moonlit Colosseum and overhears a deal: a cloaked man promises to buy a condemned shepherd’s pardon. We find out what this man can do through things he does not mean Franz to see. Power that can reach into the Pope’s own courts is far beyond a rich man’s whim.

title: The vampire
text: The Countess shudders at his pallor and calls him Lord Ruthven, a vampire. Dumas has stressed this deathly whiteness since the cave. It fits a man who was sewn into a shroud and thrown into the sea, and who climbed out alive. The joke about the undead lands closer to the truth than the Countess knows.

title: The name arrives last
text: The chapter ends with visiting cards from a neighbour called the Count of Monte Cristo. Sinbad, the island, the voice in the Colosseum and the pale man at the opera now come together under the title of the place where the treasure lay. Dumas holds back the name until we have met the man three times.

title: An eye for an eye
text: Look closely at the Count’s examples. To make his case against quick punishment, he imagines a man whose father, mother or betrothed has been destroyed. That is a precise list of what Dantès lost. He speaks as if in general, but the hatred in his face shows he is describing himself.

title: One guest eats, one guest watches
text: Albert enjoys the breakfast and the cigars. Franz notices that the host barely eats and keeps looking hard at Albert. Dumas splits our attention between two witnesses, the carefree one and the uneasy one. We know something neither of them knows: whose son Albert is.

title: A pardon staged like a miracle
text: The Count has arranged Peppino’s reprieve and watches it arrive like a god at a play. Then the murderer Andrea rages that his companion must die with him, and the Count laughs at this proof of human nature. For him, envy of another’s luck is what people are really like. He has had reason to learn that.

title: Execution as spectacle
text: Rome was then ruled by the Pope, and its executions were public, solemn and crowded, with hooded penitents in procession and the Carnival following close behind. Dumas makes us watch the death in full from a rented window, then plunges straight into the festival. It shocks Franz, and it is meant to shock us.

title: Everyone in a mask
text: Carnival is the one week when everyone in Rome goes in disguise. Albert flirts with a masked woman and is sure she must be a noblewoman. The Count changes into costume as easily as he changes names. In a book about a man in permanent disguise, Dumas has found the perfect setting.

title: From the scaffold to the confetti
text: Within hours of watching a man clubbed to death, Franz is pelting strangers with flowers. On the last night the whole Corso plays at blowing out each other’s candles. Dumas sets laughter and death side by side without comment and leaves us to feel the jolt.

title: Why does Franz want to be elsewhere?
text: The Count lends them his carriage, talks brilliantly of painting and chemistry, and never once mentions the island. Franz admires him, yet he does not want to be in Paris when the Count arrives. What exactly is he afraid of? Is it the man’s generosity, his silence, or what Franz overheard?

title: A dandy’s coolness
text: Albert is found asleep in a bandits’ lair. He thanks his rescuer politely and lights his cigar from Vampa’s torch. It is comic, and it is also a portrait of a class. A young Parisian aristocrat of 1838 is trained to treat even a death threat as a social occasion.

title: The shudder
text: Shaking Albert’s hand, the Count shudders. We know Albert’s father and mother. What does it cost this man to be thanked by that young man? And how much of the Roman adventure, from the bandits to the rescue, has he simply been watching?

title: Underground again
text: The Château d’If dungeon, the treasure grotto, Sinbad’s hidden palace, and now the catacombs: some of this book’s most important scenes take place underground. Notice how calmly the Count walks through a burial chamber full of armed men. The places that once buried him have become places where he rules.

title: Written to keep readers waiting
text: The novel first came out in installments in the newspaper Journal des Débats in 1844–46, and readers waited for each new part. An appointment fixed to the minute, three months ahead, is a serial writer’s gift. It makes a promise the reader wants to see kept, and the chapters that follow can count down to it.

title: A hand as cold as a corpse
text: When they part, the Count’s hand feels to Franz as cold as a dead man’s. It adds to the pallor and the vampire joke. Dumas keeps reminding us that this man once went into the sea as a corpse, and part of him has never come back to life.

title: Money explains everything
text: Franz tells the whole strange story, and Albert explains every part of it away. Rich men buy yachts and titles, bandits are just outlaws, and in any case the man saved his life. To Albert, great wealth makes anything believable. The Count seems to be counting on that.

title: A room as a portrait
text: Dumas lists Albert’s rooms in loving detail: every kind of tobacco, a private door, and a studio full of instruments, armor and stuffed birds left from hobbies he picked up and dropped. We learn who Albert is from his things. He is charming and indulged, and he has everything except something to do.

title: Paris under the July Monarchy
text: By 1838 France had a “citizen king,” Louis-Philippe, and a society that ran on money, newspapers and ministries. Albert’s breakfast guests are a small cross-section of it: a minister’s secretary, an opposition journalist, and soon an old-family nobleman and a soldier. The Count is about to meet the whole city through one table.

title: How did the banker know?
text: Debray has been up all night on Spanish dispatches, yet Baron Danglars somehow had the news early enough to make a million. In a world where news travels slowly, whoever hears first gets rich. How might a banker come by news before the government has finished writing it up?

title: The 5th of September
text: Morrel keeps the 5th of September every year as the day his father was miraculously saved, and he chose that day to rescue Château-Renaud. We know who sent the red purse and the new Pharaon. A private act of gratitude has become a family feast day, almost a religious one.

title: On the stroke
text: The guests laugh at the idea that the Count will turn up. Then the clock strikes half past ten and he walks in without a sound. Dumas built three months of waiting for this entrance. The Count controls even the timing of his own arrival.

title: The mask slips once
text: The Count is cool and polite with everyone until he hears Morrel’s name. Then he colors and his voice trembles. Notice what breaks his composure. It is not anger at an enemy but tenderness for the son of a friend.

title: Outside society’s protection
text: The Count says he protects no society that does not protect him. It is a calm statement of a dangerous idea: the social contract runs both ways. Think of the society that let him rot in a cell for years without a trial, and you hear what lies behind his polite tone.

title: The Catalan portrait
text: In Albert’s bedroom hangs a young woman in a Catalan fisherwoman’s dress, gazing out to sea. His father dislikes the picture, and his mother rarely looks at it without crying. The village girl of Marseilles survives only in paint, hung in her son’s room and kept away from her husband.

title: One word in a doorway
text: Dumas describes the Countess appearing pale and still in the doorway, and then the narrator simply names her: Mercédès. After so many chapters, that one word does all the work. There is no speech and no explanation, just two pale faces and a bow.

title: Flattery with a blade in it
text: The Count admires the Morcerf coat of arms “with hidden irony” and flatters the general lavishly. We know this peer of France began as a Catalan fisherman. Every compliment can be read two ways, and Dumas lets us hear the second meaning that his host cannot.

title: What does Mercédès know?
text: Lying in a darkened room, she asks Albert whether Monte Cristo is a real name and how old the Count is. His answer seems to shock her. She tells her son to be careful. What has she seen in that face, and what is she afraid of?

title: The notebook on a chain
text: For the first time we see the Count alone with his plans. He unlocks a notebook kept on a key round his neck and checks an address: “it is indeed the same.” Until now we have watched him through other people’s eyes. Here Dumas lets us see a mind at work, though not what it is working on.

title: A confession extorted
text: The Count wonders whether he can trust a confession drawn out by “religious or physical terror.” Whose confession, made to whom? He clearly knows something about his own steward that the steward does not know he knows. What does it say about the Count that he tests the truth rather than simply asking for it?

title: A house bought unseen
text: The Count claims not to know where Auteuil is, signs without a look and overpays. Then he watches Bertuccio turn pale. The purchase is a test as much as a deal. He stages even small scenes so that other people show what they are hiding.

title: A turn to the Gothic
text: Night, an empty house, a hidden staircase, a garden with a dreaded spot under a plane tree, and a servant shaking with terror. Dumas switches into the language of the Gothic novel. The house has a history, and the setting makes us feel it before anyone tells it.

title: Priest and master
text: The Count threatens Bertuccio by reminding him that the Abbé Busoni sent him and heard his confession in prison. We know who the abbé of Caderousse’s inn really was. The Count has used a priest’s role to learn men’s secrets, and now he uses those secrets as a master. Is that playing God, or something close to it?

title: Another man’s vendetta
text: Bertuccio confesses that he took Corsican blood revenge in this garden, and that his victim was M. de Villefort. A second man, with no link to Dantès, also had a score to settle with the same magistrate. Revenge in this book is not one man’s story. It runs through a whole society.

title: The same refusal, twice
text: In 1815 Villefort waved away Bertuccio’s murdered brother as a soldier of “the usurper” and refused him justice. We have seen him do this before: he judged Dantès by what served the political moment and his career. Bertuccio’s story shows that Dantès was not a single unlucky case but one victim of a pattern.

title: Buried alive
text: A box is buried in a garden at night, and inside it a newborn is barely breathing. Bertuccio digs it up and brings it back to life. The image of someone put in the ground alive and pulled out again echoes Dantès sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea. In this novel graves do not always stay shut.

title: Coincidence or design?
text: One Corsican servant turns out to have witnessed Villefort’s secret in Auteuil and Caderousse’s sale of the diamond. Dumas’s plots run on such links, and you can read them as convenience. You can also read them the way the Count does, as a hidden order in which nothing done is ever lost.

title: What did the diamond do?
text: We watched the abbé give Caderousse the diamond as a reward for telling his story. Now we hear what Caderousse and his wife did with it. Was the gift meant as a kindness, or as a test of what they were? And if it was a test, who is responsible for the result?

title: The rain of blood
text: Warm drops fall through the floorboards onto Bertuccio’s face. Minutes later he is found soaked in blood and arrested for murders he did not commit. An innocent man, marked by another’s crime and thrown in prison: the shape of Dantès’s own story returns in a new form.

title: The Count passes sentence
text: When the story ends, the Count gives his verdict. Bertuccio’s real crime, he says, was not the stabbing but failing to return the child to its mother. He also says the wicked are not so easily gone. He listens like a confessor and judges like a court. He is acting as Providence, the role he has claimed for himself.

title: The garden as a plan
text: Alone, the Count studies the garden as a “plan” laid out before him and murmurs that the prosecutor may not be dead. We cannot see the design yet, but we can feel one forming. Dumas shows us a man who looks at a crime scene the way an architect looks at a site.

title: Wealth as a weapon
text: Danglars tries to patronize the Count and offers him “even a million.” The Count calmly takes out a million in notes and shows credit on the greatest banks in Europe. He beats the banker with the only thing the banker respects. Money here is not comfort but a way to humiliate.

title: The horses
text: The Count turns Danglars away at the door, then has his prized horses bought out from under him at double the price, and arrives at the banker’s house behind them. It is a small, exact cruelty, and very public. Notice how the Count likes his gestures to be symbols that other people have to read.

title: A prisoner who owns a slave
text: The Count says Ali is not a servant but a slave whose life belongs to him. He speaks to Ali kindly, and Ali owes him his life. Even so, this is a man who spent years as the property of a prison. How does he square that past with owning another human being?

title: An accident with a rehearsal
text: The Count asks Ali whether his lasso could stop two runaway horses and posts him outside the house. At five o’clock the horses bolt past. The characters see a lucky rescue. We have been shown the preparation, so we see a design.

title: Peace in his hands
text: “The domestic peace of this family is henceforth in my hands,” the Count says as he leaves the quarrelling Danglars. He has not touched the banker’s money or his rank, only his marriage. Watch how often the Count works through households rather than through law courts.

title: The red elixir
text: One drop of a blood-red liquid brings the boy back to life. The Count warns that some of his liquids are dangerous even to smell, and he notices Madame de Villefort glance at the case. Dumas lingers on that glance. It is a pointed detail, and he wants you to register it.

title: Wishing to be Providence
text: This is the Count’s clearest statement about himself. Offered the world by Satan, he says, he asked instead to be Providence, because nothing is finer than to reward and punish. He has rewarded the Morrels and punished no one yet, but he speaks as if the bargain has been struck and he would strike it again.

title: Judge and judged, face to face
text: Villefort, the man of human law, faces the Count, who claims a higher law, and he does not recognize the young sailor he once sent away. The whole conversation is dramatic irony. When the Count says there are worse things than death, or that he was once “nearly mad,” only we know what he is talking about.

title: Who may call misfortune a punishment?
text: Villefort calls his father’s stroke God’s punishment of the old man alone, and calls his own children his reward. He reads Providence when it suits him, just as the Count does. Is there any difference between the two men’s claims to know what God intends?

title: Men who survive every regime
text: Villefort has kept his post through four revolutions. Danglars is a baron, and Fernand a general and peer. Each of the men who rose by Dantès’s fall has adapted to every change of government and come out on top. Dumas suggests that in this France, success rewards flexibility, not virtue.

title: Free, or his?
text: The Count tells Haydée that in France she is free, free even to leave him. She replies by calling him her master and saying she would die if he died. He gives her freedom, and she gives it back. What is freedom worth when one person holds all the power and the other has known nothing else?

title: Getting ready to be kind
text: The Count spends an hour with Haydée to prepare himself before visiting the Morrels. After the duel with Villefort, he needs to find a gentler self. Dumas shows him switching between roles, and suggests that the warm one now takes effort.

title: A secret named but not told
text: He asks Haydée never to speak the names of her “illustrious father” and “ill-fated mother.” Dumas tells us that there is a secret and that it matters, but not what it is. The Count is keeping her history in reserve, just as he keeps his own.

title: Relics under glass
text: The Morrels keep a silk purse, a letter signed Sinbad and a diamond under a glass cover, as a church keeps a saint’s relics. Julie says God once sent them an angel. The Count stands before the shrine to his own good deed and cannot say a word.

title: Refusing to be thanked
text: He invents a Lord Wilmore who did not believe in gratitude and has left for good. The Count could accept the thanks he has just heard. Instead he pushes it away. Why might a man who longs for justice be unable to bear being thanked?

title: “It was Edmond Dantès!”
text: Old Morrel’s last words, which the Count hears now for the first time, see through every disguise. The one person who guessed the truth did it not by evidence but by faith in a young man he had loved. The Count goes deathly pale and leaves, and his mask fails where Villefort’s suspicion could not break it.

title: Lovers from opposite camps
text: Dumas opens a love story between the son of Morrel the Bonapartist shipowner and the daughter of Villefort the royalist prosecutor. The title points to Pyramus and Thisbe, and behind them Romeo and Juliet. Two families on opposite sides of 1815 now have children who meet in secret.

title: The children inherit the quarrel
text: At Maximilian’s name, Villefort sneers at the Bonapartist Morrels of 1815, and Valentine thinks Danglars trembled. She has no idea why. We do. The fathers’ past sits in the room unspoken while their children try to plan a future.

title: Talking through a gate
text: The lovers can meet only through the planks of a boarded-up gate. Valentine describes a home where her father ignores her and her stepmother smiles and hates. Bars, walls and locked doors run all through this book, and here a rich girl’s home starts to look like one more cell.

title: A chapter made of talk
text: Almost nothing happens here except a conversation, and it is about poison. Mithridates, Eastern poisoners and a strychnine-laced cabbage passed along a chain of animals: the Count supplies the lore, and Madame de Villefort keeps steering back to it. He leaves pleased that “the seed sown” has found good soil. Dumas tells us there is a seed but not what will grow.

title: What do we owe for what we tell?
text: The Count only talks, and offers a recipe. He has watched this woman closely, from Perugia to her glance at his medicine case. How much responsibility does a person bear for knowledge handed to someone whose interests he has studied so carefully?

title: A family in one scene
text: Edward torments a parrot and tears up an album while his mother barely scolds him. Valentine comes in sad, and both children are soon sent away. At Perugia, the Count recalls, Madame de Villefort asked about Valentine’s health. Dumas sketches a whole household of favoritism in a few strokes.

title: The audience is the show
text: No one at the opera is watching the opera. They watch each other: who sits in whose box, who escorts whom, whose diamonds catch the light. Dumas uses the Paris Opéra as a stage on which society performs for itself. The Count makes his entrance there with Haydée like a leading actor.

title: Haydée’s cry
text: Haydée sees Morcerf’s face beside her guardian’s, cries out, and says this man sold her father to the Turks. We knew Fernand had betrayed Dantès. Now we learn of another betrayal, in another country, on which his fortune was built. Notice too that the Count put his arm round Morcerf at the very moment she looked across.

title: A heroine who does not want a husband
text: Eugénie Danglars is handsome, cold, gifted in music and languages, and plainly unimpressed by Albert. In a novel where young women are mostly married off, Dumas gives us one who seems to want her own life. Watch how the others describe her, as if strength in a woman were a defect.

title: A joke that hits home
text: Albert jokes that Debray, who gets government news first, should feed Madame Danglars a false report to teach her a lesson. Debray is embarrassed. The Count notices, says something quietly, and Debray answers, “Willingly, count; I accept.” Dumas shows us a deal being made without showing its terms.

title: Marriage as a merger
text: Albert does not love Eugénie, and his mother opposes the match without saying why. Their fathers got rich together in Spain, and the marriage would join two fortunes. Franz is promised to Valentine on similar terms. In this Paris, a wedding is a business arrangement between families, and the young people are the last to be asked.

title: Who is invited to Auteuil?
text: The Count plans a dinner at Auteuil for the Danglars and the Villeforts. He tactfully leaves out the Morcerfs and adds two Italian strangers. We know what happened in that garden. Why might the Count want these particular guests at that particular house?

title: Directing an actor
text: The “major” is not sure he was a major, is surprised by his own wealth, and only believes his son is called Andrea. The Count feeds him every line and produces every document. It is pure comedy, and it shows the Count as a playwright and director, casting and rehearsing his players.

title: A past made of paper
text: A marriage certificate, a baptism record, a uniform with medals waiting at the hotel: Cavalcanti’s noble past arrives in a parcel. Dumas makes a sharp point about the society the Count is entering. If papers and money are what count, then rank can be bought and a whole family history forged.

title: Why a fake nobleman?
text: The Count already has wealth and a title of his own. Why does he need a borrowed Italian aristocrat, a lost son and a story about a kidnapping? What could such a pair do in Paris that the Count could not do himself?

title: The peephole
text: The Count watches the “reunion” through a hidden peephole, and the two men embrace like actors on a stage. He is the only audience for his own play. Then they compare notes and drop the act, and we see that neither knows what part he has really been cast in.

title: Providence works with forgers
text: The Count calls them two scoundrels and says it is a pity they are not really related. The man who claims to be an agent of Providence has chosen a forger and a fraud as his tools. Is that a contradiction, or does he think the wicked are the right instruments for punishing the wicked?

title: Sinbad signs again
text: Andrea’s letter of introduction is signed “Sinbad the Sailor,” and the Count explains Sinbad away as Lord Wilmore. These are the very names behind the Morrels’ rescue. The same aliases now open doors for an impostor, and the Count’s masks serve both mercy and design.

title: The danger of being an heiress
text: Valentine has her mother’s fortune and expects more from her grandparents. Her stepmother quietly encouraged her to become a nun, which would have sent it all toward little Edward. Valentine’s wealth does not protect her. It makes her someone else’s obstacle.

title: Two readings of one man
text: Maximilian has known the Count barely ten days but feels bound to him, and thinks he lost at cards on purpose so Maximilian could buy his horse. Valentine distrusts him as her stepmother’s friend, a man who has never looked at her. Each judges from what they have seen, and given what each has seen, each is reasonable. Dumas lets the Count look different from every angle.

title: Eugénie’s wish
text: Valentine reports that Eugénie almost wishes her father would lose his fortune, so that she could be free to live as an artist. For most people in this novel money is the goal. What does it mean that one young woman sees it as a cage?

title: Imprisoned in a body
text: Noirtier can move only his eyes. Remember Faria, struck down by paralysis in his cell, and Dantès buried alive in the Château d’If. Here is another mind locked in a prison, this time his own body. Yet through blinks, an alphabet and a dictionary, the helpless old man becomes the most forceful will in the room.

title: A name from 1815
text: The groom is Franz de Quesnel, Baron d’Épinay, and his father was assassinated in 1815. The name Quesnel should ring a bell from Noirtier’s talk with his son in Paris. Villefort speaks pointedly of an old political hatred, and Noirtier answers with contempt. The quarrels of the Hundred Days are being settled through the grandchildren.

title: Father and son, still at war
text: Villefort gave up his father’s name and politics to rise under the king. Now he rarely visits the paralyzed old man and talks over him as if he were furniture. The split between the Bonapartist father and the royalist son, first seen in Marseilles, has become a cold war under one roof.

title: The lawman beaten by law
text: Villefort, the great prosecutor, watches his speechless father prove his mind is sound to two notaries and dictate a will. Dumas enjoys turning legal form against the man who has always used it as a weapon. Villefort cannot even contest the will, because a man in his position cannot be seen to go to court against the poor.

title: Money as a voice
text: Noirtier cannot speak, walk or write. His fortune is the only power he has left, and he uses it to speak. He disinherits the granddaughter he loves to stop a marriage she does not want. In a society that listens to money, 900,000 francs is a louder voice than any words.

title: Why is she glad?
text: The chapter closes on three faces: Valentine weeps, Villefort bites his lips, and Madame de Villefort cannot hide her joy. The money is going to the poor, not to her son. So why is she so pleased?

title: Why hurry the wedding?
text: The Count advises Villefort to settle Valentine’s marriage the moment Franz returns, so that it cannot be undone. Villefort is grateful, and his wife changes color. Why should the Count care whom Valentine marries, or how quickly?

title: “Some gloomy legend”
text: The Count names his address, Rue de la Fontaine, No. 28, and Villefort goes pale. Then the Count teases that if Villefort stays away he will suspect the house has a gloomy legend. Thanks to Bertuccio, we know the legend. Every light word in this scene lands on a man who has no idea how much his host knows.

title: A lonely tower on the Spanish line
text: The Count says he is going to see a telegraph, and he chooses an isolated station on the line to Spain rather than an official one. Remember that Danglars made a million from early Spanish news, and that Debray accepted something from the Count. What could a man want with the machine that carries the government’s news?
